content: Rocky Mountain spotted fever (RMSF) is the most severe tick-borne rickettsial illness in the United States. It is caused by an infection with the bacterium Rickettsia rickettsii. Patients infected with Rickettsia rickettsii typically seek medical attention during the first week of illness, following an incubation period of approximately 5 to 10 days after a tick bite. The early symptoms of RMSF are often nonspecific and can mimic other infectious or non-infectious diseases. Initial symptoms may include fever, nausea, vomiting, muscle pain, loss of appetite, and severe headache. As the disease progresses, additional symptoms such as rash, abdominal pain, joint pain, and diarrhea may develop. The classic triad of fever, rash, and a history of tick bite is important for diagnosis, although not all patients present with all three components at the time of their initial medical evaluation. RMSF can be a severe illness, and most patients require hospitalization. The causative organism, Rickettsia rickettsii, is transmitted through the bite of an infected tick. In the United States, the primary tick vectors are the American dog tick (Dermacentor variabilis) and the Rocky Mountain wood tick (Dermacentor andersoni). The brown dog tick (Rhipicephalus sanguineus) has also been implicated as a vector, as has the tick Amblyomma cajennense in regions south of the United States. Certain populations are at higher risk for RMSF. The disease is more frequently reported in males, Caucasians, and children, with two-thirds of cases occurring in children under the age of 15, particularly those aged 5 to 9 years. RMSF is a seasonal disease, with most cases occurring between April and September. Over half of the cases are reported in the South Atlantic region of the United States, with the highest incidence rates in North Carolina and Oklahoma. Despite its name, relatively few cases are reported from the Rocky Mountain region today. The diagnosis of RMSF is based on a combination of clinical signs and symptoms, as well as specialized laboratory tests. Common laboratory findings that may support the diagnosis include thrombocytopenia (low platelet count), hyponatremia (low sodium levels), and elevated liver enzyme levels. Untreated RMSF can lead to life-threatening complications. The treatment of choice for RMSF is the antibiotic doxycycline, a tetracycline-class drug. Adults are typically prescribed 100 mg every 12 hours, while children weighing less than 45 kg (100 lbs) are dosed at 4 mg/kg per day in two divided doses. Treatment should continue for at least three days after the fever resolves and until there is clear evidence of clinical improvement. The standard duration of treatment is 5 to 10 days. Because laboratory confirmation is often unavailable during the acute phase of illness, treatment is initiated based on clinical and epidemiological findings. Several other diseases may present with symptoms similar to RMSF, including babesiosis, Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever, Lyme disease, Southern tick-associated rash illness (STARI), and tick-borne relapsing fever. Individuals in tick-infested areas should wear light-colored clothing to make ticks more visible, tuck pant legs into socks to prevent ticks from crawling inside, and use tick repellents. Permethrin-based repellents can be applied to clothing and boots, while DEET-based repellents can be applied to the skin. DEET should be used cautiously in children. After spending time in tick-prone areas, individuals should perform thorough body checks using a mirror to identify and remove any attached ticks. Pets and clothing should also be inspected for ticks, as they can carry ticks into the home. If a tick is found attached to the skin, it should be removed promptly and carefully. Proper tick removal techniques are essential to minimize the risk of disease transmission. The prognosis for RMSF is generally favorable with timely treatment. Most patients recover fully, but complications can occur in severe cases. These complications may include paralysis, hearing loss, nerve damage, brain damage, clotting disorders, heart failure, kidney failure, lung failure, meningitis, pneumonitis, and shock. Sources for this information include the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and MedlinePlus.
